chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) who said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to me, who said: Yaqoob ibn Yazid narrated to me, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Khalid, from Abu Hamza al-Thumali, from Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon them both) who said:

"I do not like to possess red-haired camels (a symbol of great wealth) instead of my being oppressed; I have never quenched my thirst (found greater satisfaction) than quenching my wrath by not retaliating against the one who angered me."

key_terms.بِذَلِّ نَفْسِي: My being oppressed/humbled, referring to enduring hardship or injustice
key_terms.جُرْعَةِ غَيْظٍ: Quenching of wrath/anger, metaphorically referring to the satisfaction of suppressing anger
key_terms.حُمُرُ النَّعَمِ: Red-haired camels, a classical idiom for great wealth or valuable livestock
key_terms.لَا أُكَافِئُ بِهَا صَاحِبَهَا: Not retaliating against the owner/oppressor, meaning forgiving or not returning the evil

ai.seo_question: What is the virtue of suppressing anger and enduring oppression according to Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Khisal*, Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (AS) highlights the immense spiritual value of *sabr* (patience) and *kzm al-ghadab* (restraining anger), prioritizing inner peace over material wealth symbolized by 'red-haired camels.' This teaching underscores the Shia emphasis on emotional mastery as a key characteristic of the righteous, where refraining from retaliation is viewed as a higher form of worship than acquiring worldly riches. The narration serves as a practical guide for believers to cultivate nobility of character by absorbing injustice with grace rather than seeking immediate recompense.
